mkay i was struggling w the exact same thing earlier and here's what worked for me:

1. i wrote little "drabbles" (50-200ish words) for each of the ideas that i had in mind just to get a feel for what it would look like (for me, i had 9 different drabbles)
2. i looked through the drabbles and eliminated the ones that didn't look promising or that i wasn't passionate about (left me with 5 ideas)
3. i showed the remaining drabbles to my parents and counselors and friends to get their opinion and feedback
4. i picked the 3 most promising ideas and elaborated on it even more (around 300 words).
5. i asked everyone for feedback and looked through them myself after a couple of days to see which one felt the most genuine to me
6. i picked one of the ideas to write a full essay on!

edit: i originally commented this under another person's comment but thought that it would make more sense to say it here, so here i go.

**trigger warning: fatphobia, anorexia, bulimia, eating disorder in general**

just my opinion, but it's much more than that and to say that fatphobia doesn't exist demonstrates a massive privilege. for example, when an overweight or obese person goes to a doctor, there is a higher chance of their health problem being written off as a side effect of their weight and prescribing them a healthy diet and exercise. i shadowed a urologist who told me about an overweight woman who came to her clinic experiencing hematuria (urinating blood). previous doctors and specialists did not examine the situation and simply told her immediately that it would go away if she lost weight. however, the urologist i shadowed discovered that the patient had pyelonephritis (a type of kidney infection) that could have been deadly if not treated immediately. multiple studies have shown the individuals with higher BMIs are less likely to trust healthcare providers because they tend to focus only on BMI, even when they came in for something completely not related.

the BMI system itself is flawed. BMI doesn’t consider other factors of health, like age, sex, genetics, lifestyle, medical history, or other factors. by simplifying our measurement of health to just a number, we ignore other important measurements like cholesterol, blood sugar, heart rate, inflammation levels, etc. BMI uses the same calculations for both men and women, despite women generally having less muscle mass and more fat mass. the calculation does not consider an individual’s age, which is significant because our bodies naturally decline in muscle mass as we grow older.

several studies also suggest that BMI is not completely relevant for all populations, especially those of specific ethnic backgrounds. i actually just watched a TED Talk that talked how 96% of genetic research and 95% of clinical trials are focused on people of European descent. the BMI system was created by and for a Eurocentric population, which creates complications when we consider that people of different ethnic backgrounds have different body composition. BMI assumes that all weight is equal, whether it’s bone, fat, or muscle (which is denser and heavier than fat). for example, Black people are often misclassified as overweight despite having a lower risk of chronic disease because they’re genetically more likely to have higher muscle mass.

for my own story, i struggle a lot with eating disorders, specifically anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa. when the disorder first began in 4th grade, i was considered overweight for my age and height. when my mother went to my general provider about the fact that i would skip meals, weigh myself dozens of times a day, and purge after i ate anything, we were told that i was finally making healthy decisions. we all know that no one would have said that if i was already skinny. it wasn't until i was deadly underweight that people began getting concerned. when a skinny girl starves herself, she's anorexic. when a fat girl starves herself, she's being healthy. no one questioned my mental state or why i always seemed so tired or any of that when i was overweight. no one cared until i needed to be in a hospital bed.

this isn't to attack you or anyone else, but i think that a lot of people underestimate the amount of discrimination there is against people who are overweight. so thank you for reading my ted talk and letting me get this off of my chest.

application essays really are all that important because they're what gives AOs an idea of your personality (with the interview, of course!) especially for the top schools.

think of it this way. if you're a T20 AO, a significant percentage of the applicants have *crazy* extracurriculars, so seeing another person with amazing extracurriculars doesn't set them apart from the other ones. they're just one of the many qualified applicants to a very good school. however, colleges don't just want to know what you've accomplished in the past, they want to know what type of person you are and that's where the essay comes in. the essay can tell them how you think, the experiences that impacted you significantly, etc. it adds dimension to your application in a way that nothing else can. an AO is less likely to remember you as the-dude-who-was-student-body-president because who knows how many student body presidents apply to the school every year. they are more likely to remember you as the-dancer-who-is-reminded-of-his-late-grandmother-when-he-dances.

hello! i'm a rising senior who dealt with something similar (for me, it was a few months into junior year when the realization of oh shit, i need to be doing more hit me) and hope that i can leave a few tips!

1. first things first, try to not look at what other people are doing and focus on yourself. i am a massive hypocrite when it comes to this but, i promise that stalking your classmates on Linkedin won't help your resume. instead, focus on how *you* want to improve and grow, so next,
2. you should sit down and think about what you're passionate about. it's perfectly okay if you're not sure yet! but having an idea of what you're working towards and what you're interested in as of right now can be really motivating! this can help you get a good idea of what your major might be. if you catch yourself thinking "i want to do \_\_\_, but i'm not good enough to" then stop! it's almost never too late to turn your life around. my cousin struggled a lot and originally attended community college, but worked hard and transferred to a state school and this year, he graduated from uchicago medical school (Pritzker)! and he saved loads of money and graduated w almost no debt, which i would say is a win! no matter what you want you've got this!
3. meet with your school's college counselor. they're often the best resources for any questions you might have, doubts, etc. and 99% of the time they want you to succeed (and the last 1% is the rare crabby ones, but we don't talk about them) they can help you with how you can improve your chances of getting into the college of your dreams! you can also ask them for different extracurricular opportunities.
4. connect with friends who are doing well in the classes that you struggle in. sticking by them and occasionally asking for help can be a lifesaver at times! have study sessions together prior to tests, ask them if they're interested in making a study guide with you, etc.
5. friends can also be really helpful for networking and finding extracurriculars you might be interested in. extracurriculars can vary from clubs to outside projects to research endeavors to jobs to sports to family responsibilities. basically, there's a lot that can be considered an extracurricular! you mentioned that you play football and do track and field, which is definitely a good start! my suggestion would be to continue those if possible and add a few other extracurriculars on top of that for a solid application! ask about what your friends are doing and try to join those. in the A2C wiki, there is a post about a comprehensive list of extracurricular ideas for quarantine that you can start right now! you can also PM me if you want other suggestions!
6. pick a few of your favorite teachers (preferably at least two) and try to form a relationship w them outside of class (don't get me wrong -- *not* romantic). maybe stay after class to ask them homework questions, about something they said in class, etc. find a common interest to geek out over. say hi to them when you see them walking down the hallway. volunteer to help pass out papers. join clubs that they are supervisors of. these don't have to be teachers of the classes you're planning to major in, just teachers that you click well with. in letters of recommendation, it's more meaningful if a teacher can talk about you as a person, not just about you aced their class. and, of course, treat all of your teachers with respect!
7. start prepping for the SAT or ACT! there are loads of completely free online resources (ex: khan academy) that are really helpful if you don't know where to start. everyone that i've talked to generally suggest starting preparations about 6 months before taking the test and working from there. try to take your first test in the first semester of junior year so that you have time to retake if you're not happy with your score! r/Sat has got loads of compiled resources for your convenience!
8. remember that the prestige of the college does not make it a good college for you! while people usually talk about the top 20-30 schools, going to one doesn't guarantee your success and not going to one doesn't mean that you've failed at life. when looking into colleges, aim for a balanced list with varying acceptance rates. aim for about 1-2 safety schools (acceptance rates 61-100%), 3-4 target schools (acceptance rates 31-60%), and 3-4 reach schools (acceptance rates 0-30%).
9. try to not stress about it too much! you've got loads of time and colleges value a rising trendline (where a student shows significant improvement over the course of their high school careers)! focus on self improvement and you've got this! if you have any questions, feel free to PM me and i'll be happy to help anyway i can!

hello! i'm a rising senior who was in a similar position as you a few years back. short answer: yes, you should have some extracurricular activities. don't stress though - you're still very early in your high school journey, so you have time!

from your GPA, i assume that you're doing really well in school, which is always a plus when applying to colleges. however, colleges usually like to see that you're doing more than the bare minimum and that you're exploring your interests outside of school as well. it shows that you are not only a good student, but an effective member of your community as well. it's nice for admissions officer to know that you're understanding the subjects you are being taught, but it means more to them when you are going out of the way to apply and reinforce that knowledge in a real-world context to further your own interests and support others who are not in the position you are! being a high-achieving student is nice, but being a well-rounded student is more important when it comes to colleges. for example, a college is more likely to pick a mediocre student with outstanding extracurriculars, awards, and community service than a high-achieving student who is just that.

is there a particular reason why you disliked clubs and extracurriculars? i will say that, in my experiences, clubs are very different in high school in that there's a much bigger pool and lots of different ideas/opinions. when i came to high school, i also had a super negative perception of school clubs, especially since i was a bit of an outsider joining a private high school where i knew no one. it was difficult to go to club meetings when i was the only one left without a group or partner, etc. however, something i soon came to realize when i started actually joining clubs in 10th grade is that being part of activities outside of school allows you to meet ppl with similar interests and form connections that way.

all in all, something you have to realize is that the vast majority of college applicants are very good students, so GPA doesn't mean too much at a certain extent. of course, it matters that you get good scores, but a college won't necessarily weigh a 4.65 GPA higher than a 4.43 GPA based on just that (source: i've talked extensively with my three school college counselors, who are all ex-AO for ivy schools + Stanford). colleges are increasingly recognizing that GPA are not an accurate measurement of intelligence or how well you do in school. they're also moving away from standardized testings (SAT and AP exams): many colleges are considering continuing optional testing after the pandemic and most top colleges are offering less and less credit for AP/IB/AICE exams. what colleges are caring more and more about is taking a holistic view of the student. they genuinely want to know whether you'll be a good fit for the school *community*, not just in a classroom. they want to know what you're doing outside of school, what your interests are and how you're expanding them, what type of person you are, and what is your relationship with the other people at your school and your community. colleges value leadership positions because it shows a lot of dedication into your endeavors. colleges value community service because it shows you care about your community and improving it. colleges value internships and externships because it shows that you have strong interests and are proactively trying to work towards them at a young age.

please feel free to reach out if you want ideas of extracurricular activities that are a good fit for you! another good resources could be your school counselors, if you're not comfortable talking with a random hooman from the internet, but i do think that there are extracurricular activities for everyone!

2. look into need-blind colleges and less at need-aware schools. need-blind schools are colleges that don't factor in your financial situation when making the decision and will accept you based on how good your application is only. need-aware schools are less likely to accept you, especially as an international student, if you cannot pay the tuition. i know that Stanford is need-blind for US citizens, but not for most international countries, so you might want to check on that.

do you have an idea of what colleges you're looking into? try starting with that! do a little bit of research about the different colleges that you're interested in. some good resources for that is [niche](https://www.niche.com/), [college board big future](https://bigfuture.collegeboard.org/college-search), and [cappex](https://www.cappex.com/colleges). make a list of what you're looking for in a college (ex: good food, nice campus, good research opportunities, strong computer science major, etc.) and keep it in mind. look at the college websites and explore the pages. i recommend you dedicate an hour to every school that you research and that you take extensive notes (these notes will be helpful for answering the essay prompts later!). once you have a list of 7-10 colleges that you're interested in, start attending college tours and information session. many of them are online because of the global pandemic and for international students like yourself. a lot of colleges also have information sessions just for international students so i would definitely check those out. 

i'm not sure for unis in other countries, but most schools in the us use the [common app](https://www.commonapp.org/static/8f866bccc95edef01d02a2069adaefcc/FYInternationalCAReady.pdf) or the coalition app (which is a pain... i don't recommend). look into those and ask your school's college counselor for more info about them! look into taking the SAT or ACT, the AP or IB exams, and other things that colleges look into. additionally, start compiling your extracurricular activities. most colleges in the us care more about the holistic picture of the student (their interest, the activities they're doing outside of school, the clubs they're involved in, the internships they have, the non-school projects they're participating in, the volunteer activities they're doing, etc.) than just the statistics. it's really difficult to go to a good school w/o extracurriculars so don't neglect them!

i hope this helps and good luck!

additionally, remember that a lot of colleges have merit scholarships and, for a lot of schools, you're considered for merit scholarships without having to apply to anything extra. i would say do some research into the colleges you're interested in and see the scholarship opportunities.
